summaries.example: Imagine riding in a car while thinking hard about a game. You may still steer around a corner, because your eyes and brain are taking in information. Later, you might realize you did not notice the road very much. A higher-order theory says that seeing the road may have happened without becoming a conscious experience because you were not aware of that seeing. When you notice a color or a feeling, a further mental representation may make the first state conscious.
summaries.summary: Higher-order theories try to explain why some mental states are conscious while others are not. They focus on phenomenal consciousness: the felt part of seeing, hearing, feeling, or thinking. The main idea is that a first mental state becomes conscious when another mental state is directed at it. This second state might be like an inner perception, or it might be a thought such as “I am seeing red.” Some theories say the higher-order state must actually occur. Others say the first state only needs to be ready to produce one. Self-representational theories say that a conscious state represents itself as well. The entry also explains objections. A theory must address cases in which people act on information without awareness, cases in which higher-order representation seems to occur without a real first-order state, and questions about rocks, animals, and babies. The source presents these disagreements without treating them as settled.
key_ideas: The entry separates being conscious as a creature from having a conscious mental state.
Higher-order theories say that a thought or perception can be unconscious until another mental state represents or monitors it.
Some versions use a perception-like inner sense; others use a thought about one’s own mental state.
The theories are debated, especially over animals, infants, false awareness, and whether higher-order representation really explains feeling.
summaries.why_it_matters: Consciousness affects how we understand minds, feelings, perception, animals, infants, and the brain. Higher-order theories offer a way to connect a personal feeling—such as seeing a color—with mental processes that can be studied. They also show why explaining consciousness is difficult: a theory must explain both the information a mind uses and the felt point of view of the person or creature.

important_terms.definition: Being awake or able to respond, in the broad sense. This is different from asking whether a particular thought, feeling, or sight is conscious.
A mental state having a special felt quality—there is something it is like to have it, such as seeing red or feeling pain.
A mental state that can guide thinking, choosing, remembering, or acting, whether or not it has a felt quality.
A mental representation about another mental state. The higher-order state is called “higher” because it is about a lower-level state.
The idea that a mental state becomes conscious when the mind is, in some suitable way, aware of that state.

questions_to_think_about: Can you do something well without paying attention to it? Does that show that some mental work can be unconscious?
Is thinking about a feeling the same as having the feeling?
Could an animal have a felt experience without thinking about its own mind?
What would count as a good explanation of consciousness?

summaries.example: Suppose you look at two nearly identical drawings and notice a small extra dot in one. You may consciously see the dot without consciously judging, “This is the feature that makes the drawings different.” A higher-order thought theorist can distinguish these two claims: the visual state may be the target of a higher-order representation without your having a further conscious thought about the comparison itself. This illustrates why awareness of a mental state need not be the same as explicitly knowing what that state is about.
summaries.summary: Higher-order theories explain the difference between conscious and unconscious mental states by appealing to a representation directed at the state in question. The motivation is that many kinds of mental state—perceptions, beliefs, desires, pains, and emotions—seem able to occur without consciousness. Phenomenally conscious states, by contrast, have a subjective character: there is something it is like to be in them. Higher-order perception theories propose an inner monitoring system that produces perception-like representations of first-order states. Actualist higher-order thought theories propose that a first-order state becomes conscious when it non-inferentially causes a thought about itself. Dispositionalist versions require only a suitable availability to higher-order thought. Self-representational and hybrid theories instead treat self-representation as part of the conscious state or as integrated with it. Critics question whether higher-order representation is necessary or sufficient, whether it creates false or targetless consciousness, and whether it explains the distinctive feel rather than merely describing awareness. The entry also surveys implications for animals and infants and the debate about prefrontal neural mechanisms.
key_ideas: The central target is phenomenal consciousness, not merely wakefulness or information that can guide behavior.
Higher-order perception theory appeals to a perception-like monitoring process, while HOT theories appeal to thoughts about mental states.
Actualist and dispositionalist HOT theories disagree about whether a higher-order thought must occur or only be available.
Self-representational and hybrid theories challenge the assumption that first-order and higher-order states must be separate.
Major objections concern computational complexity, misrepresentation, targetless higher-order states, animals and infants, and whether the theory explains felt experience.
Neuroscientific versions often connect higher-order processing with the prefrontal cortex, but the location and necessity of such processing remain disputed.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate connects a first-person phenomenon—subjective experience—to cognitive architecture and neuroscience. It helps clarify why being awake, being able to use information, introspecting, and having a felt experience are not automatically the same thing. The theories also have consequences for how we think about nonhuman and infant consciousness, although the source emphasizes that these consequences depend on controversial assumptions about the required kind of higher-order representation and its neural basis.

important_terms.definition: A property of a mental state consisting in its subjective character: what it feels like to undergo the state.
A form of consciousness defined by a state’s functional availability for reasoning, decision-making, memory, or action.
A representation directed at another mental representation or mental state, such as a thought that one is seeing red.
The proposal that a conscious state is one of which its subject is aware in an appropriate way.
The theory that conscious states are produced when an inner, perception-like system represents first-order perceptions.
The actualist view that a mental state is conscious when it actually causes a suitable higher-order thought, normally without conscious inference.
The view that a state is conscious because it is available or disposed to produce a suitable higher-order thought, even if that thought is not occurring.
A family of views on which the conscious state itself also represents or presents itself, either as one state with two roles or as an integrated part-whole complex.

questions_to_think_about: If a person thinks they are in pain when there is no first-order pain state, is there a conscious pain experience or only a mistaken thought?
Does a state need to be available for reasoning to be conscious, or is a felt quality possible without such access?
Would a simple higher-order representation be enough for animal consciousness, or would it require sophisticated concepts?
Why might a theory distinguish seeing a dot from seeing that the dot is the difference between two pictures?
What evidence would separate brain activity involved in consciousness from activity involved only in attention or reporting?

summaries.example: You are practicing a basketball move while chatting with a friend. Your eyes may guide your hands and feet even though you are not paying attention to every detail. Later, you notice the bright lights in the gym and the feeling of your shoes on the floor. A higher-order theorist might say that the first information guided your actions without being conscious, while the noticed sights and feelings became conscious because your mind represented them in a further way.
summaries.summary: The entry examines higher-order approaches to consciousness. It first distinguishes several uses of “conscious”: an organism may be awake, aware of an object, or undergoing a mental state with a subjective feel. The theories mainly address the last question. Their basic proposal is that a perception, thought, desire, pain, or emotion becomes phenomenal when a further mental representation is directed at it. Higher-order perception theory describes this further representation as an inner-sense-like perception. Higher-order thought theories describe it as a thought about being in the first-order state. Actualist HOT theory requires the thought to occur; dispositionalist HOT theory requires only a suitable readiness for it to occur. Other theories combine or identify the first-order and higher-order aspects. The approach is motivated by examples such as automatic driving and blindsight, where information seems to guide behavior without ordinary awareness. However, critics challenge whether higher-order representation is needed, whether it can misrepresent or lack a target, and whether it can explain the actual feel of experience. The source also discusses questions about animal and infant consciousness and possible links to prefrontal brain activity.
key_ideas: Consciousness can mean being awake, being aware of something, or having a mental state with a felt quality; these meanings should not be mixed together.
Higher-order theories focus mainly on state consciousness and claim that awareness of a mental state helps make it phenomenal.
Some theorists compare higher-order awareness to an inner sense; others describe it as a thought about one’s own experience.
Theories differ over whether the higher-order state must actually happen, merely be possible, or be part of the original state itself.
Opponents ask whether unconscious perception, blindsight, and action-guiding vision really show that mental states can be unconscious.
The debate includes difficult cases involving mistakes, animals, infants, and the brain systems involved in conscious experience.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because it asks what changes when a mental process becomes part of conscious experience. The answer could shape theories of perception, emotion, self-awareness, rational thinking, and the minds of other creatures. It also encourages careful thinking about evidence: behavior alone may not reveal whether a state is conscious, and brain activity associated with reporting or attention may not be identical to the neural basis of experience.

important_terms.definition: The condition of an organism being awake, or being aware of something in the world. Philosophers distinguish this from consciousness belonging to a particular mental state.
The felt side of a mental state: the fact that seeing, hearing, pain, or emotion can feel like something from the subject’s point of view.
A kind of consciousness involving a state’s availability for reasoning, decisions, memory, or behavior.
A mental state that represents or is directed toward another mental state, such as a thought about one’s own seeing.
The claim that a conscious mental state is one that the subject is aware of in an appropriate manner.
An account that treats awareness of first-order perceptions as produced by an additional, perception-like monitoring system.
A higher-order thought theory requiring an actual, suitably caused thought about a first-order mental state.
A higher-order thought theory requiring that a mental state be ready or available to produce a thought about itself, even when that thought is not currently present.

questions_to_think_about: Can information guide behavior without producing a conscious experience?
Would a thought about pain be enough to create pain if no first-order pain state existed?
Does being aware of an experience require a concept such as “experience”?
Why might thinking about a rock differ from representing your perception of the rock?
Should evidence about brain regions decide between competing theories of consciousness?
